15 CFR Parts 732, 734, 740, 742, 743, 744, 748, 762, 772, and 774
[Docket No. 261116-0005]
RIN 0694-AK50

Bureau of Industry and Security, Department of Commerce.

Interim final rule.

In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)—countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

Effective date:
This rule is effective November 19, 2026.
Comment due date:
Comments on the revisions and additions in this rule must be received by BIS no later than January 19, 2027.

Comments on this rule may be submitted to the Federal rulemaking portal (

All filers using the portal should use the name of the person or entity submitting the comments as the name of their files, in accordance with the instructions below. Anyone submitting business confidential information should clearly identify the business confidential portion at the time of submission, file a statement justifying nondisclosure and referring to the specific legal authority claimed, and provide a non-confidential version of the submission.
For comments submitted electronically containing business confidential information, the file name of the business confidential version should begin with the characters “BC.” Any page containing business confidential information must be clearly marked “BUSINESS CONFIDENTIAL” on the top of that page. The corresponding non-confidential version of those comments must be clearly marked “PUBLIC.” The file name of the non-confidential version should begin with the character “P.” Any submissions with file names that do not begin with either a “BC” or a “P” will be assumed to be public and will be made publicly available through
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Commenters submitting business confidential information are encouraged to scan a hard copy of the non-confidential version to create an image of the file, rather than submitting a digital copy with redactions applied, to avoid inadvertent redaction errors which could enable the public to read business confidential information.

For general questions, contact Timothy Mooney, Director, Regulatory Policy Division, Office of Exporter Services, Bureau of Industry and Security, U.S. Department of Commerce at 202-482-2440 or by email:

.

In this IFR, BIS is amending the EAR (
15 CFR parts 730-774
) to establish new controls to ensure that computing power, based on U.S. technology located in foreign data centers, is not used in a manner contrary to U.S. national security or foreign policy interests. This IFR accomplishes this by:
Adding an end-use control requiring a license for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) of advanced SI
[
1
]
items when there is “knowledge” the items are destined for use in data centers, wherever located, that will provide direct or indirect access to a significant volume of computing power to or for an entity headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, Macau or destination specified in Country Group D:5. License applications will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. These changes are contained in new § 744.24(a)(1). In addition, if subsequent to the original
(
printed page 74971)
export of advanced SI semiconductors to an overseas data center, that data center starts providing, directly or indirectly, significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered, or with an ultimate parent headquartered, in Macau or Country Group D:5, the owner, operator of the overseas data center, or other party making the transfer will be required to obtain a license. Any data center providing significant volume of compute power to companies headquartered, or with an ultimate parent headquartered, in Macau or Country Group D:5 prior to the publication date of this rule that wishes to continue providing these services must obtain a license with 90 days of the effective date of this IFR or face future export restrictions. However, the license requirement will not apply to `commercial recommender systems,' such as those used by online retailers and social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat.
This new control is a logical extension of existing controls. At present, a license is required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced SI semiconductors for entities headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, Country Group D:5 or Macau. Through this rule, BIS is imposing restrictions that will undermine those entities' ability to access significant volumes of advanced SI semiconductors remotely, including through connected cloud computing.
Adding a destination-based license requirement for advanced SI items for destinations for which there is an unacceptable risk of diversion—which for the purposes of this IFR are Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brazil, and Thailand. See amendments to § 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A)(
1
).
Rescinding the worldwide Regional Stability (RS) license requirement and other regulatory changes implemented by the AI Diffusion rule, “Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion” published January 15, 2025 (
90 FR 4544
) (“AI Diffusion Rule”).
By making these changes, this IFR prevents the use of certain SI items in data centers and at a computing power level that can be used for training or running of advanced SI models. Access to such computing power can be used to train and run advanced SI models capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten U.S. national security or foreign policy interests,
e.g.,
using advanced SI for developing more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.
Specifically, BIS is enhancing and streamlining the licensing policy on items controlled under Export Control Classifications Numbers (ECCNs) 3A090 and 4A090 and the corresponding .z items by using a combination of more focused and effective destination-based controls and enhanced end-use controls. This IFR amends the EAR to reflect a revision to the license review policy for these items in parts 742 (Regional stability) and 744 (Control Policy: End-User and End-Use Based) to simplify the licensing process for SI integrated circuits (ICs) and other SI-related items. The changes promulgated in this IFR follow extensive U.S. government consideration of the impact of these controls on U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

This IFR revises § 742.6 to impose new license requirements and licensing policies for advance computing items identified in paragraph (a)(6)(iii)(A).
First, under § 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A)(
1
), a license is required for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to or within Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brazil, and Thailand. As noted in section I of this preamble, these countries are being added in response to concerns that advanced computing items subject to EAR licensing requirements are being diverted to entities and countries of concern without authorization. See section III of this preamble for a discussion of those controls.
The license requirements for items described in § 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A)(
1
) do not apply to exports, reexports, and transfers (in-country) to an ultimate consignee or end user headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided the reporting requirements of new § 743.10, described in section VI of this preamble, are met by the exporter, reexporter, or transferor. This is explained under new Note 1 to paragraph (a)(6)(iii)(A)(
1
) of § 742.6.
Second, under § 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A)(
2
), this IFR amends the worldwide licensing requirement to require a license for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to or within destinations specified in Country Groups D:1, D:4, and D:5, excluding destinations specified in Country Groups A:5 or A:6, as well as the United Arab Emirates—to the extent a license would otherwise be required by the final rule “Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations” (
91 FR 43034
, July 14, 2026).
For the license requirements under paragraph (a)(6)(iii)(A)(
1
) of § 742.6, applications for exports, reexports, and transfers (in-country) will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis to determine whether the transaction is contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States, as described under § 742.6(b)(10)(iii)(A)(
1
). Pursuant to § 742.6(b)(10)(iii)(A)(
1
), destinations will be evaluated on the effectiveness of their export control regimes and their coordination with BIS on the enforcement of export controls.

This IFR adds new § 744.24 Restrictions on exports, reexports, and transfers (in-country) of certain advanced computing items for use in data centers for end-uses and destinations of concern. Section 744.24 provides, in addition to the license requirements set forth elsewhere in the EAR, a prohibition on exports, reexports, or transfers (in-county) of advanced SI items without a license if, at the time of export, reexport, or transfer (in-country), you have “knowledge” that the item will be or is intended to be used in a data center end-use that is prohibited under paragraphs (a)(1) of § 744.24.
You may not knowingly export, reexport, or transfer (in-county) items specified in paragraph (a) of § 744.24 for use in a data center to or within any destination worldwide that will provide access to more than 12,000,000 “aggregate TPP” (either at one data center or through `linked data centers' (including digitally-linked infrastructure, not just physically-linked infrastructure) to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, Macau or a destination specified in Country Group D:5 in supplement no. 1 to part 740 of the EAR. `Linked data centers' are data centers that use networking infrastructure that links two or more separate data centers together to allow physical and virtual facilities to share resources, balance workloads, and replicate data as a unified whole. This prohibition is described under § 744.24(a)(1) and the definition is provided in § 744.24(d). The term “for an entity” as used in this § 744.24(a)(1)
(
printed page 74972)
applies to instances in which there is “knowledge” that a data center is providing remote access to a non-D:5 customer that is in turn training SI models for, or participating in the training of SI models for, or providing SI models to a D:5 company. This control will cut off additional potential diversion pathways and evasion efforts.
These controls are necessary because providing computer power access at this level or greater will allow for training or running of advanced SI models; the Secretary of Commerce has determined that it could pose a national security and foreign policy threat to the United States when such computing power access will be provided to or for companies headquartered, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, Macau or a destination specified in Country Group D:5—unless the computing power is exclusively used for commercial recommender systems. Access to advanced computing power presents significant national security and foreign policy concerns, primarily by enabling foreign countries or other entities of concern to accelerate the development of weapons of mass destruction (WMD), execute sophisticated zero-day cyberattacks on critical infrastructure, and disrupt global military balances of power—unless the computing power is exclusively used for commercial recommender systems.
Consistent with the national security and foreign policy concerns outlined in this IFR, BIS is imposing a notification and authorization requirement for subsequent changes in end-use. This requirement, provided in new paragraph (e) of § 744.24, and described in more detail further in this section, is triggered if there is a change in end-use of the items described in paragraph (a)(1) of § 744.24. In the event of such a change, a BIS authorization may be required. Relatedly, Note 1 to paragraph (a)(1) of § 744.24 provides that the prohibition applies regardless of whether the person in possession of the EAR item was a party to the transaction to the original export, reexport, or transfer (in-country),
i.e.,
the original shipment of the items to the data center. Because this EAR end-use control under § 744.24(a)(1) applies to any subsequent reexport or transfer (in-country), including changing from a non-prohibited end-use to a prohibited end-use, it is important that parties in possession of these items are aware of the need to review § 744.24(a)(1) for any subsequent reexport or transfer (in-country).
The prohibition described in paragraph (a)(1) applies regardless of whether a U.S.-origin item specified under paragraph (a) of § 744.24 has been incorporated or commingled into or with a foreign-made item. Reexporters and transferors may not rely on the
de minimis
provisions for incorporating or commingling U.S.-origin items specified under paragraph (a) of § 744.24 into foreign-made items where there is “knowledge” at any point in the chain from the development, production, or use of the foreign-made item that the U.S.-origin item will be used in this prohibited end-use under paragraph (a)(1) of § 744.24. This prohibition under § 744.24 is described under Note 2 to paragraph (a)(1).
Note 3 to paragraph (a)(1) describes due diligence expectations imposed on “U.S. persons” and foreign data centers to ensure compliance with these controls. Foreign data centers will be expected to perform robust due diligence on their customers to identify direct or indirect ownership or control by Country Group D:5 or Macau persons. This diligence will ensure that companies cannot circumvent new controls through corporate restructurings or spinoffs.
This IFR adds an “is informed” process under paragraph (a)(2) of § 744.24 to impose an additional prohibition on persons informed by BIS that a license is required for the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of specified items to certain persons or destinations, because there is an unacceptable risk of use in, or diversion to, the activities specified in paragraph (a)(1) of § 744.24. Notifications made under paragraph (a)(2) that there is an unacceptable risk of use in, or diversion to an end use specified in § 744.24 may be made either individually by specific notice or through amendment to the EAR.
As described under § 744.24(b), no license exceptions may overcome the prohibition described in paragraph (a)(2) of § 744.24, except when noted by BIS. The prohibitions under § 744.24 do not apply when the computing power access is being provided exclusively for a `commercial recommender system' under the (b)(2) exception provided the reporting requirements described therein are followed.
Applications for licenses required by § 744.24 will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis as described under § 744.24(c).
This IFR adds paragraph (d) to define for purposes of § 744.24 the terms: `linked data centers'; and `commercial recommender system':
For purposes of § 744.24, `linked data center' means a data center that uses networking infrastructure that links two or more separate data centers together that allows physical and virtual facilities to share resources, balance workloads, and replicate data as a unified whole. This includes digitally-linked infrastructure, not just physically-linked infrastructure.
For purposes of § 744.24, `commercial recommender system' means a Super Intelligence (SI) tool exclusively designed and exclusively used to rank, filter, or suggest commercial products, services, or content to users based on user behavior, transaction history, or item attributes. This term does not include any SI system designed or used to generate novel text, image, audio, video, software, or other content in response to user inputs, or any system that incorporates such model, regardless of whether the system also performs recommendation functions.
This IFR adds paragraph (e) to impose a notification and authorization requirement for subsequent changes in end-use. New paragraph (e) specifies that for any export, reexport, or transfer made on or after November 19, 2026 without a license,
i.e.,
because the exporter, reexporter, or transferor had no “knowledge” that the item is for a prohibited end-use under this section and no other EAR license requirement applies, the exporter, reexporter, or transferor must inform the recipient that BIS authorization is required if the item will be transferred in-country; and that the recipient must follow the know-your-customer guidance in supplement no. 3 Part 732 of the EAR. The notification also must specify that the transferor,
e.g.,
the data center operator, must obtain authorization for this change in end-use. Changes in end-use from a non-prohibited end-use to a prohibited end-use under paragraphs (a)(1) are considered a “transfer (in-country)” for purposes of paragraphs (a)(1) or (2) and require an EAR authorization under § 744.24.

This IFR, as described under section II of this preamble, removes the worldwide license requirement from former § 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A). As a conforming change, this IFR makes revisions to the advanced computing items end-use control under § 744.23(a)(3) to ensure that a license will continue to be required for exports, reexports, and transfers (in-country) of these advanced computing items when such items are destined for entities headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, Country Group D:5 or Macau.
(
printed page 74973)
Specifically, this IFR revises § 744.23 “Supercomputer,” “advanced-node integrated circuits,” and semiconductor manufacturing equipment end-use controls under paragraph (a)(3)(i)(A) to specify that this end-use control for advanced computing items includes all advanced computing items (
e.g.,
those specified in ECCNs 3A090 (except for 3A090.c), 4A090, and related .z paragraph items). Prior to this IFR, there was an enforced license requirement under § 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A) of the EAR that applied to all destinations outside of the United States for these advanced computing items when such items are destined to entities headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, Country Group D:5 or Macau.
See
the May 31, 2026, “Guidance Regarding Enforcement of License Requirements for Advanced Computing Items for Entities Headquartered in Country Group D:5 and Macau” on the BIS website at
http://www.bis.gov
.
With the removal of the worldwide license requirement this IFR makes a required conforming change to return the license requirement for these advanced computing items to § 744.23(a)(3)(i)(A).
For § 744.23(a)(3)(i)(A), BIS has received inquiries regarding the meaning of the phrase “for an entity” that is headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, either Macau or a destination specified in Country Group D:5. As stated in BIS's October 2023 Advanced Computing/Supercomputing (“AC/S”) IFR (
88 FR 73458
) this control was intended to ensure that the national security and foreign policy objectives of the October 7, 2022 IFR and the AC/S IFR are not undermined by Macau, the People's Republic of China (PRC), or other Country Group D:5 headquartered entities setting up cloud servers or data centers in other countries to allow these entities of concern to continue to train their SI models in ways that would be contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. This end-use control thus is not, and has never been limited only to exports, reexports, and transfers (in-country) destined to such entities of concern as ultimate consignees or end users, but extends to exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country)
on behalf of
these entities of concern,
e.g.,
if an entity of concern was the purchaser in the transaction (directly or indirectly) or was the exclusive or primary (greater than 50 percent of total compute) remote end user of the data center computing capacity. Exporters, reexporters, and transferors are encouraged to examine both end-use controls in § 744.23(a)(3) and in new § 744.24 to the extent their transactions involve exports, reexports, or transfers to data centers outside of the United States where there is knowledge that a company headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent is headquartered in, Macau or D:5 will be an intended remote end user. Any entities in violation of this requirement should submit a voluntary self-disclosure (see Section 764.5 of the EAR). Bona fide operators of data centers who are otherwise engaged in activities consistent with the EAR and were providing remote access used for `commercial recommender systems' (as defined in the new § 744.24(d)(1)) may continue providing these services for 90 days, but must obtain a license following expiration of this period to continue these services. Finally, § 744.23(a)(3)(i)(C) is added to create a license requirement for “applicable advanced node integrated circuits” that are subject to the EAR, specified in 3A090.a, designed by a company that is neither an approved IC designer (specified in supplement no. 6 to part 740) or an authorized IC designer (as described in Note 1 to 3A090.a), and exported, exported from abroad, reexported, or transferred (in-country) by a “front end fabricator” or “OSAT” to or within any destination. This addition ensures that a license requirement continues to apply to “front end fabricators” and “OSATs” creating advanced ICs for non-approved, non-authorized IC designers wherever located. Additionally, the presumption created in Note 1 to 3A090.a continues to apply but can be overcome by the “front end fabricator” or “OSAT” if they follow the due diligence steps specified in that note. BIS notes that the inclusion of the phrase “exported from aboard” in this new paragraph is simply descriptive and not intended to indicate that the activity of exporting from destinations other than the United States is not captured in provisions of the EAR where that phrase is omitted.

This IFR revokes the controls on model weights published in the AI Diffusion Rule. BIS has determined that a more effective approach to address national security and foreign policy concerns that arise from the transfer of model weights is through the use of specified destination-based or end-use license requirements. Accordingly, ECCN 4E091 is removed from the CCL in supplement no. 1 to part 774. This IFR also makes the necessary conforming changes to other parts of the EAR to remove references to ECCN 4E091 and model weights by: (1) removing Red Flag 28 in supplement no. 3 to part 732; (2) removing the AI Model weights Foreign Direct Product (FDP) rule in § 734.9; (3) removing reference to 4E091 from § 740.2; (4) removing the RS license requirement text that applies to AI model weights in § 742.6; (5) removing 748.3(f); and (6) removing the definition of “Model Weights” in § 772.1.

This IFR revokes the tiers of countries created in the AI Diffusion Rule and the final rule for “Expansion of Validated End User Authorization: Data Center Validated End User Authorization,”
89 FR 80080
(Oct. 2, 2024), which were implemented through License Exception Artificial Intelligence Authorization (AIA) in § 740.27, supplement no. 5 to part 740, the Data Center Validated End-Users (VEU) Authorization in § 748.15 and supplement no. 8 to part 748 (including reverting the reference to General VEU Authorization to use VEU Authorization wherever the term is used).
Specifically, this IFR removes License Exception AIA from the EAR by: (1) removing reference to this license exception in § 740.2; (2) reserving § 740.27 for future use; (3) removing supplement no. 5 to part 740; and (4) removing AIA from ECCNs in supplement no. 1 to part 774 when listed in the list-based license exceptions section. This IFR removes the Data Center VEU Authorization from § 748.15, supplement no. 8 to part 748, and supplement no. 10 to part 748. This IFR also makes conforming changes to the license review policy in § 742.6 to remove references to supplement no. 5 to part 740.

(1) Removing License Exceptions AIA from § 740.2 Restrictions on all License Exceptions;
(2) Removing License Exceptions Artificial Intelligence Authorization (AIA) (§ 740.27) and License Exception Low Processing Performance (LPP) (§ 740.29) from the EAR;
(3) Removing references to the revoked License Exceptions AIA and LPP (formerly in § 740.27 and § 740.29) and adding the notification and authorization requirements in the new § 744.24 in § 762.2 Records to be retained; and
(
printed page 74974)
(4) Removing references to the revoked License Exceptions AIA, and LPP (formerly in § 740.27 and § 740.29) from the CCL.

BIS is retaining the worldwide destination scope of the advanced computing foreign direct product (FDP) rule in § 734.9(h)(2)(i) if there is “knowledge” that a foreign-produced item is destined worldwide or will be incorporated into any “part,” “component,” “computer,” or “equipment” not designated EAR99 to any location worldwide. Retention of this provision ensures the prohibitions of relevant controls are not otherwise limited.
Though BIS is not making any changes to § 734.9(h), BIS notes that the agency has received questions about the application of that paragraph. Consistent with the robust controls implemented in this IFR, BIS notes that provision's expansive application. If a foreign-produced product is subject to the EAR pursuant to § 734.9(h), BIS retains jurisdiction of that item after its incorporation into another foreign-produced item, as provided by the text of § 734.9(h)(2)(i). For example, if an ECCN 3A090 IC is incorporated into a foreign-produced “part,” “component,” “computer,” or “equipment” (such as a GPU board or server), BIS continues to have jurisdiction over the IC and license requirements may apply to the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of the IC (and by extension, the server). Generally, BIS does not retain jurisdiction over items after incorporation into other items, absent the applicability of the EAR's
de minimis
provisions. But in this context, specifically, in the relevant ECCN entries (ECCN 4A090 and those ECCNs with a .z paragraph), the CCL notes that such items only meet the specifications for those ECCNs if they contain an ECCN 3A090 IC. Thus, even third parties who only receive a 4A090 item are on notice that such items contain an ECCN 3A090 IC. Furthermore, the retention of BIS's jurisdiction under § 734.9(h) after incorporation is reflected by past BIS guidance to inform parties in the supply chain of the applicability of the FDP rule, including the Model Certification for Purposes of the FDP Rule of supplement no. 1 to part 734 of the EAR.
In addition, consistent with the removal of ECCN 4E091, this IFR removes the AI Model weights FDP rule in § 734.9(l).

BIS is retaining License Exception ACM under § 740.28 due to the benefits this license exception plays in supporting the supply chains of export, reexports, and transfers (in-country) of advanced SI items destined to ultimate end users outside of Macau or destinations in Country Group D:5.

This IFR also changes the presumptions faced by front-end fabricators and OSAT companies defined in Note 1 to 3A090.a. Specifically, paragraphs b. and c. of Note 1 to 3A090.a are amended to remove eligibility to overcome the presumption in Note 1 to 3A090.a for an integrated circuit designer located in or having an ultimate parent headquartered in a destination specified in Country Groups D;1, D:4, or D:5 of supplement no. 1 to part 740 of the EAR or in paragraph (a)(6)(iii)(A)(1) of § 742.6. Such companies which are not Authorized or Approved IC designers and face a presumption that their IC is 3A090.a for all “applicable advanced logic integrated circuits”. This addresses potential diversion pathways of advanced ICs.

In addition to the changes described in Sections II and III, this IFR makes conforming changes to the EAR due to the changes described in this preamble.

For a transaction to be excluded from the license requirements of § 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(
1
), the exporter, reexporter, or transferor must comply with the reporting requirement introduced by this IFR in new § 743.10 Reporting Requirements to Qualify for Exclusion from Certain Regional Stability Requirements. The reporting requirement mitigates the risk that transactions excluded from this license requirement will be used or diverted contrary to the EAR by allowing the U.S. Government to monitor the items being exported, reexported, or transferred (in-country).
New § 743.10 describes in paragraph (b) the information to be included in the report; in paragraph (c), where to submit the report; in paragraph (d), the timeframe as to when reporting is required; and in paragraph (e), contacts for general information or questions about this report.

In addition to removing the definition for “model weights” described in section IV.A. of this preamble, this IFR adds a definition to § 772.1 for “Aggregate TPP” to describe the sum TPP of a group of ICs or commodities.

Due to the revisions to the RS reason for control under § 742.6 made in this IFR, conforming revisions are made to ECCNs: 3A001, 3A090, 3D001, 3E001, 4A003, 4A004, 4A005, 4A090, 4D001, 4D090, 4E001, 5A002, 5A992, 5A004, 5D002, 5E002, 5E992, and 5D992. For these ECCNs, the reason for control table is revised by removing references to items paragraphs 3A090.a and .b, 4A090.a and .b, and the corresponding .z paragraphs. Additionally, the reference to the worldwide RS license requirement in the control tables is revised with a new reference that a license is required to or within any destination specified in § 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A) of the EAR.

Add § 744.24 to read as follows:
(a)
General prohibition
—(1)
Prohibition on exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) for certain advanced computing items for use in data centers for end uses of concern.
In addition to the license requirements set forth elsewhere in the EAR, you may not export, reexport, or transfer (in-county) items specified in ECCNs 3A001.z; 3A090 (except for 3A090.c); 3D001 (for “software” for commodities controlled by 3A001.z, 3A090 (except for 3A090.c)); 3E001 (for “technology” for commodities controlled by 3A001.z, 3A090 (except for 3A090.c)); 4A003.z; 4A004.z; 4A005.z; 4A090; 4D001 (for “software” for commodities controlled by 4A003.z, 4A004.z, and 4A005.z); 4D090 (for “software” for commodities controlled by 4A090); 4E001 (for “technology” for commodities controlled by 4A003.z, 4A004.z, 4A005.z, 4A090 or “software” specified by 4D001 (for 4A003.z, 4A004.z, and 4A005.z), 4D090 (for “software” for commodities controlled by 4A090)); 5A002.z; 5A004.z; 5A992.z; 5D002.z; 5D992.z; 5E002 (for “technology” for commodities controlled by 5A002.z or 5A004.z or “software” specified by 5D002 (for 5A002.z or 5A004.z commodities)); or 5E992 (for “technology” for commodities controlled by 5A992.z or “software” controlled by 5D992.z) without a license if you have “knowledge” at the time of the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) that the item is destined to a data center to or within any destination worldwide that is providing or will provide access to more than 12,000,000 “aggregate TPP” either at one data center or through `linked data centers' to or for companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, Macau or a destination specified in Country Group D:5 in supplement no. 1 to part 740 of the EAR.

The prohibitions pursuant to paragraph (a)(1) apply regardless of whether the person in possession of the EAR item was a party to the transaction to the original export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) (see § 748.5).

The prohibitions pursuant to paragraph (a)(1) apply regardless of whether a U.S.-origin item specified under paragraph (a) of this section has been incorporated or commingled into or with a foreign-made item. Reexporters and transferors may not rely on the de minimis provisions for incorporating or commingling U.S.-origin items specified under paragraph (a) into foreign-made items where there is “knowledge” at any point in the chain from the “development”,
“production”, or “use” of the foreign-made item that incorporates or commingles a U.S.-origin item will be used in a prohibited end-use under paragraph (a)(1) of this section.

To satisfy the requirement that you do not have “knowledge” for purposes of this paragraph, you will be expected to obtain and be able to provide sufficient information from the foreign data center regarding that data center's “know your customer” due diligence checks. Such diligence checks will include diligence on whether any data center customers are subject to direct or indirect ownership or control by persons located in, headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent is headquartered in, Macau or a destination specified in Country Group D:5. A foreign data center declining or being unable to provide information sufficient to verify compliance with this end use control shall be considered a red flag that presumptively provides you with “knowledge” unless you are able to resolve that red flag before proceeding with the transaction.
(2)
Additional prohibition on persons informed by BIS.
BIS may inform persons, either individually by specific notice or through amendment to the EAR, that a license is required for the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of specified items to certain persons or destinations, because there is an unacceptable risk of use in, or diversion to, the activities specified in paragraph (a)(1) of this section. Specific notice is to be given only by, or at the direction of the Secretary of Commerce or the Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security. When such notice is provided orally, it will be followed by a written notice within two working days signed by the Secretary of Commerce or the Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security. However, the absence of any such notification does not excuse persons from compliance with the license requirements of paragraphs (a)(1) of this section. The Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs may notify the Secretary of Commerce that a certain destination is at high risk of use in, or diversion to, the activities specified in paragraph (a)(1) of this section. Within 10 days of receipt of such notice, the Secretary of Commerce shall, if he deems it appropriate, inform persons, either individually by specific notice or through amendment to the EAR, that a license is required for the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of specific items to that destination.
(b)
Exceptions.
(1) No license exceptions may overcome the prohibition described in paragraph (a) of this section, except as noted by BIS when a destination is designated under paragraphs (3) of this section.
(2) The prohibitions under this section do not apply when the computing power access is only being provided for a `commercial recommender system' and you submit the following information to
https://www.bis.gov/​ai/​exclusionnotesubmission
,
which will be shared with the End User Review Committee.
(i) The name of the company headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, Macau or a destination specified in Country Group D:5 in supplement no. 1 to part 740 of the EAR.
(ii) The sum of the total processing performance (TPP, as defined in the Technical Notes to ECCN 3A090) of all of the ICs or commodities specified in paragraph (a)(1) provided to or for the company specified in (b)(2)(i).
(iii) The due diligence performed to ensure the computing power access is exclusively being provided for a `commercial recommender system.' (3) Any data center providing significant volume of compute power to companies headquartered, or with an ultimate parent headquartered, in Macau or Country Group D:5 prior to the publication date of this rule that wishes to continue providing these services must obtain a license with 90 days of the effective date of this IFR or face future export restrictions.
(c)
License review policy.
Applications for licenses required by this section will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis.
(d)
Definitions.
For purposes of this section, the following definitions are applicable:
(1)
Commercial recommender system.
A commercial recommender system means a Super Intelligence (SI) tool exclusively designed and exclusively used to rank, filter, or suggest commercial products, services, or content to users based on user behavior, transaction history, or item attributes. This term does not include any SI system designed or used to generate novel text, image, audio, video, software, or other content in response to user inputs, or any system that incorporates such model, regardless of whether the system also performs recommendation functions.
(
printed page 74979)
(2)
Linked data center.
For purposes of this section, a `linked data center' means a data center that uses networking infrastructure that links two or more separate data centers together, through digitally-linked or physically-linked infrastructure, that allows physical and virtual facilities to share resources, balance workloads, and replicate data as a unified whole. `Linked data center' includes digitally-linked infrastructure, not just physically-linked infrastructure.
(e)
Notification and authorization requirement for subsequent changes in end-use.
For any export, reexport, or transfer made on or after November 19, 2026 without authorization,
i.e.,
because the exporter, reexporter, or transferor had no “knowledge” that the item is for a prohibited end-use under this section and no other EAR license requirement applies, the exporter, reexporter, or transferor must inform the recipient that a BIS authorization is required if the item or items will be used at a data center to provide access to more than 12,000,000 “aggregate TPP” either at one data center or through `linked data centers' to or for companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, Macau or a destination specified in Country Group D:5 in supplement no. 1 to part 740 of the EAR. The notification from the exporter, reexporter, or transferor must also specify that the transferor,
e.g.,
the data center operator, must obtain authorization for this change in end-use. The notification from the exporter, reexporter, and transferor must also specify that the transferor must follow the know-your-customer guidance in supplement no. 3 Part 732 of the EAR.

VEU Authorization permits the export, reexport, and transfer (in-country) to validated end-users of any eligible items that will be used in a specific eligible destination. To be eligible for authorization VEU, exporters, reexporters, and validated end-user applicants must adhere to the conditions and restrictions set forth in paragraphs (a) through (f) of this section. If a request for VEU authorization for a particular end-user is not granted, no new license requirement is triggered. In addition, such a result does not render the end-user ineligible for license approvals from BIS.
(a)(1)
Eligible end users for VEU Authorization.
The only end users to whom eligible items may be exported, reexported, or transferred (in-country) under a VEU Authorization are those validated end users identified in supplement no. 7 to part 748, according to the provisions in this section and those set forth in supplement nos. 8 and 9 to this part that have been granted VEU status by the End-User Review Committee (ERC) according to the process set forth in supplement no. 9 to this part.
(2)
Requests for authorizations.
To apply for a VEU Authorization, requests for authorization must be submitted in the form of an advisory opinion request, as described in § 748.3(c), and must include a list of items (items for purposes of authorization VEU include commodities, software, and technology, except as excluded by paragraph (c) of this section), identified by ECCN, that exporters, reexporters, or transferors intend to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) to an eligible end user, once approved. To ensure a thorough review, requests for VEU authorization must include the information described in supplement no. 8 to this part. Requests for authorization will be accepted from exporters, reexporters, transferors, or end-users. Submit the request to: The Office of Exporter Services, Bureau of Industry and Security, U.S. Department of Commerce, 14th Street and Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Room 2099B, Washington, DC 20230. Mark the package “Request for “General” Authorization Validated End-User.”
(c) * * *
(1) Items controlled under the EAR for missile technology (MT) and crime control (CC) reasons may not be exported or reexported under a VEU Authorization.
(e)
Certification and recordkeeping.
Prior to an initial export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) to a validated end-user under a VEU Authorization, exporters, reexporters, and transferors must obtain certifications from the validated end-user regarding end-use and compliance with VEU requirements. Such certifications must include the contents set forth in supplement no. 8 to this part. Certifications and all records relating to VEU must be retained by exporters, reexporters, or transferors in accordance with the recordkeeping requirements set forth in part 762 of the EAR.
(f)
Reporting and review requirements
—(1)
Reports
—(i)
Reexport Information Required for VEU authorization.
Reexporters or transferors who make use of a VEU Authorization are required to submit annual reports to BIS. For VEU authorization, reexporters and transferors must include, for each validated end user to whom the exporter, reexporter, or transferor exported, reexported, or transferred (in-country) eligible items:
(A) The name and address of each validated end-user to whom eligible items were exported, reexported or transferred (in-country);

(D) The value of such items; and
(E) The ECCN(s) of such items.
(ii) [Reserved]
(iii)
Deadlines.
For reexporters or transferors making use of VEU Authorization, reports are due by February 15 of each year, and must cover the period from January 1 through December 31 of the prior year.
(iv)
Addresses.
Reports must be sent to: Office of Exporter Services, Bureau of Industry and Security, U.S. Department of Commerce, 14th Street and Constitution Avenue NW, Room 2099B, Washington, DC 20230. Mark the package “General Authorization Validated End-User Report.”
(2)
Reviews.
Records related to activities covered by VEU Authorizations that are maintained by exporters, reexporters, transferors, and VEU authorizations will be reviewed on a periodic basis. Upon request by BIS,
(
printed page 74980)
exporters, reexporters, transferors, and validated end-users must allow review of records, including on-site reviews covering the information set forth in paragraphs (e) and (f)(1) of this section.
(g)
Notification requirement.
Exporters, reexporters, and transferors shipping under VEU Authorization are required to provide the VEUs to which they are shipping notice of the shipment. Such notification must be conveyed to the VEU in writing and must include a list of the VEU-authorized contents of the shipment and a list of the ECCNs under which the VEU-authorized items in the shipment are classified, as well as a statement that the items are being, will be, or were shipped pursuant to relevant VEU Authorization. Notification of the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) to the VEU must be made within a timeframe agreed to in writing by the VEU and the person exporting, reexporting or transferring (in-country). The VEU and the person exporting, reexporting, or transferring (in-country) must agree to the notification timeframe prior to the initial shipment under the VEU Authorizations. Depending on the agreement between the VEU and the person exporting, reexporting, or transferring (in-country), a notification may be for individual shipments or for multiple shipments. Exporters, reexporters, transferors, and VEUs are required to maintain the notifications they send or receive in accordance with their recordkeeping requirements.
(h)
Termination of Conditions on a VEU Authorization.
VEUs that are subject to item-specific conditions and have received items subject to such conditions under General VEU Authorization are no longer bound by the conditions associated with the items if the items no longer require a license for export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) to or within the PRC or India, as applicable, or become eligible for shipment under a license exception to the destination. Items that become eligible for a license exception are subject to the terms and conditions of the applicable license exception and the restrictions in § 740.2 of the EAR. Items that become eligible for export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) without a license and that remain subject to the EAR may only be exported, reexported, transferred (in-country), or disposed of in accordance with the requirements of the EAR. Termination of VEU conditions does not relieve a validated end-user of its responsibility for violations that occurred prior to the availability of a license exception or prior to the removal of license requirements.
(i)
Records.
Records of items that were shipped under VEU Authorization prior to the removal of a license requirement or the availability of a license exception remain subject to the review requirements of paragraph (f)(2) of this section on and after the date that the license requirement was removed or the license exception became applicable.

Technical Note 1 to 3A090.a:
The `approximated transistor count' of a die is the `transistor density' of the die multiplied by the area of the die measured in square millimeters. The `transistor density' of the die is the number of transistors that can be fabricated per square millimeter for the process node used to manufacture the die. To calculate the number of `approximated transistor count' of a die, a “front end fabricator” or “OSAT” company has two options. First, the “front end fabricator” or “OSAT” company may take the transistor density of the process node used to manufacture the die and multiply this density by the area of the die. This number may be significantly higher than the true transistor count, but if the result is below the relevant transistor threshold, then the “front end fabricator” or “OSAT” company can be confident that the die in question will not exceed that threshold. Second, to adjudicate edge cases, the “front end fabricator” or “OSAT” company may use standard design verification tools to estimate the number of (both active and passive) transistors on the die using the GDS file.

Technical Note 2 to 3A090.a and 3A090.b:
1. `Total processing performance' (`TPP') is 2 × `MacTOPS' × `bit length of the operation', aggregated over all processing units on the integrated circuit.
a. For purposes of 3A090, `MacTOPS' is the theoretical peak number of Tera (10
12
) operations per second for multiply-accumulate computation (D = A × B + C).
b. The 2 in the `TPP' formula is based on industry convention of counting one multiply-accumulate computation, D = A × B + C, as 2 operations for purpose of datasheets. Therefore, 2 × MacTOPS may correspond to the reported TOPS or FLOPS on a datasheet.
c. For purposes of 3A090, `bit length of the operation' for a multiply-accumulate computation is the largest bit-length of the inputs to the multiply operation.
d. Aggregate the TPPs for each processing unit on the integrated circuit to arrive at a total. `TPP' = TPP1 + TPP2 + . . . . + TPPn (where n is the number or processing units on the integrated circuit)
.
2. The rate of `MacTOPS' is to be calculated at its maximum value theoretically possible. The rate of `MacTOPS' is assumed to be the highest value the manufacturer claims in a manual or brochure for the integrated circuit. For example, the `TPP' threshold of 4800 can be met with 600 tera integer operations (or 2 × 300 `MacTOPS') at 8 bits or 300 tera FLOPS (or 2 × 150 `MacTOPS') at 16 bits. If the integrated circuit is designed for MAC computation with multiple bit lengths that achieve different `TPP' values, the highest `TPP' value should be evaluated against parameters in 3A090.
3. For integrated circuits specified by 3A090 that provide processing of both sparse and dense matrices, the `TPP' values are the values for processing of dense matrices (e.g., without sparsity).
4. `Performance density' is `TPP' divided by `applicable die area'. For purposes of 3A090, `applicable die area' is measured in millimeters squared and includes all die area of logic dies manufactured with a process node that uses a non-planar transistor architecture
.
c. High bandwidth memory (HBM) having a `memory bandwidth density' greater than 2 gigabytes per second per square millimeter.
Technical Note 1 to 3A090.c:
‘Memory bandwidth density’ is the memory bandwidth measured in gigabytes per second divided by the area of the package or stack measured in square millimeters. In the case where a stack is contained in a package, use the memory bandwidth of the packaged device and the area of the package. High bandwidth memory (HBM) includes dynamic random access memory integrated circuits, regardless of whether they conform to the JEDEC standards for high bandwidth memory (HBM), provided they have a `memory bandwidth density' greater than 2 gigabytes per second per square millimeter. This control does not cover co-packaged integrated circuits with both HBM and logic integrated circuit where the dominant function of the co-packaged integrated circuit is processing. It does include HBM permanently affixed to a logic integrated circuit designed as a control interface and incorporating a physical layer (PHY) function.

a.1. Items having “information security” as a primary function;
a.2. Digital communication or networking systems, equipment or components, not specified in paragraph 5A002.a.1;
a.3. Computers, other items having information storage or processing as a primary function, and components therefor, not specified in paragraphs 5A002.a.1 or .a.2;
N.B.: For operating systems see also 5D002.a.1 and .c.1.
a.4. Items, not specified in paragraphs 5A002.a.1 to a.3, where the `cryptography for data confidentiality' having a `described security algorithm' meets all of the following:
a.4.a. It supports a non-primary function of the item;
and
a.4.b. It is performed by incorporated equipment or “software” that would, as a standalone item, be specified by ECCNs 5A002, 5A003, 5A004, 5B002 or 5D002.
N.B. to paragraph a.4: See Related Control Paragraph (4) of this ECCN 5A002 for examples of items not controlled by 5A002.a.4.

1. For the purposes of 5A002.a, `cryptography for data confidentiality' means “cryptography” that employs digital techniques and performs any cryptographic function other than any of the following:
1.a. “Authentication;”
1.b. Digital signature;
1.c. Data integrity;
1.d. Non-repudiation;
1.e. Digital rights management, including the execution of copy-protected “software;”
1.f. Encryption or decryption in support of entertainment, mass commercial broadcasts or medical records management; or
1.g. Key management in support of any function described in paragraphs 1.a to 1.f of this Technical Note paragraph 1.
2. For the purposes of 5A002.a, `described security algorithm' means any of the following:
2.a. A “symmetric algorithm” employing a key length in excess of 56 bits, not including parity bits;
2.b. An “asymmetric algorithm” where the security of the algorithm is based on any of the following:
2.b.1. Factorization of integers in excess of 512 bits (e.g., RSA);
2.b.2. Computation of discrete logarithms in a multiplicative group of a finite field of size greater than 512 bits (e.g., Diffie-Hellman over Z/pZ); or
2.b.3. Discrete logarithms in a group other than mentioned in paragraph 2.b.2 of this Technical Note in excess of 112 bits (e.g., Diffie-Hellman over an elliptic curve); or
2.c. An “asymmetric algorithm” where the security of the algorithm is based on any of the following:
2.c.1. Shortest vector or closest vector problems associated with lattices (e.g., NewHope, Frodo, NTRUEncrypt, Kyber, Titanium);
2.c.2. Finding isogenies between Supersingular elliptic curves (e.g., Supersingular Isogeny Key Encapsulation); or
2.c.3. Decoding random codes (e.g., McEliece, Niederreiter).
Technical Note:
An algorithm described by Technical Note 2.c. may be referred to as being post-quantum, quantum-safe or quantum-resistant.

sections.heading: AGENCY:
sections.content: Bureau of Industry and Security, Department of Commerce.

sections.heading: ACTION:
sections.content: Interim final rule.

sections.heading: SUMMARY:
sections.content: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)—countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.
